d.title: Nine terms, and the one number that dates the whole list
d.caption: Every term above the line is a decision about **what a token is and how many of them there are**; every term below it is a decision about **how a token becomes a number**. The perplexity row is the one that shows how far the field moved: **a good trigram model sits near 80 and a modern LLM near 3–10**, which is the same metric reporting an order-of-magnitude different world.

d.title: Four tokens, four different fates, from one regex
d.caption: The pattern is a single character class and it draws four different lines. **`didn't` survives whole because the apostrophe is inside the class; `e-mailed` is split in two because the hyphen is not.** Neither outcome was chosen — both fell out of one decision about which characters count as word characters. Which is the lesson: **preprocessing destroys information you did not decide to destroy**, and the only way to know what it did is to print it.

d.title: Two opposite sentences, one identical output
d.caption: This is the measurement that decides the question, and it is not a matter of degree: **“this movie is not good” and “this movie is good” both reduce to `movie good`.** The stopword list contains *not*, so the one word carrying the sentiment is the one removed — **and the classifier downstream cannot recover it, because the two inputs are now the same string.** The question-answering row loses *who* and *of*, which is most of the question's structure.

d.title: Fifteen types to ten, and what survives tells you the rest
d.caption: **A 33% smaller vocabulary from one `.lower()` call** — and that is the whole argument for preprocessing: fewer parameters to learn and more examples per type, which mattered enormously when the model was a linear classifier over sparse counts. **Read what survives, though: `cat` and `cats` are still two types, and `sat` and `sitting` are still two.** Case was the cheap half; morphology is what stemming and lemmatisation are for.

state: A / a, The / the, CAT / cat

d.title: Six eras, and the pipeline got shorter as the model got bigger
d.caption: The bars are eras rather than durations, and the trend is the point: **every stage of hand-built preprocessing in this lesson was invented for the era where the model was a linear classifier over sparse counts.** Rule-based meant regexes and CFG parsers; statistical meant Naive Bayes, SVM, CRF and HMM; then Word2Vec and GloVe, then ELMo, then BERT and T5, then GPT-4 and Claude. **As the model absorbed more of the work, the pipeline in front of it shrank** — so most of what this lesson measures is now a decision you make about the input rather than a step you must run.

d.title: The emoji is where this pipeline and the reference part
d.caption: One input, two outputs, and **`match: False`** — the reference's expected string drops the emoji and this pipeline keeps it. Which is worth stopping on rather than fixing silently: **nothing in the stage list says what to do with an emoji, so the answer depends on whether your punctuation class happens to include it.** For sentiment that is a real decision, because 🎉 carries more signal than most of the words around it.

d.title: Eight stages on one string, each one printed
d.caption: Read the `$30.50` column: **it survives every stage until punctuation removal turns it into `3050`** — a price became a four-digit integer, and no stage announced it. The ellipsis is the other one worth noting: **NFKD turned `…` into three full stops, so a Unicode normalisation step silently changed the character count**, which matters the moment you are tracking spans or offsets back into the original text.

d.title: Four ordering constraints, and each has a specific victim
d.caption: The stages are **not commutative**, and the reasons are mechanical rather than stylistic. **`https://user@host/path` contains an `@`, so an email pattern run before the URL pattern butchers it.** HTML before URLs, or the URL regex eats `href` attribute values and leaves broken tags. **And lowercasing is a one-way door for every case-sensitive pattern you have not run yet** — acronym detection, proper-noun heuristics and `RT` stripping all stop working.

d.title: Seven words, and the stemmers agree on the ones that do not matter
d.caption: They agree on `running`, and the interesting rows are where they do not. **`studies` becomes `studi` in both — not a word, and that is fine, because a stemmer's output is an index key rather than text.** `generously` splits them: Porter cuts to `gener`, Snowball stops at `generous`. **And the three failures are shared: `better`, `children` and `mice` pass through untouched**, because suffix-chopping cannot do irregular morphology at all.

d.title: The part-of-speech tag is the whole difference
d.caption: `better` with `pos="a"` becomes **good**; `running` with `pos="v"` becomes **run** — exactly the two words the stemmers could not touch. But read what the lemmatiser needs to get there: **a dictionary lookup, and a part-of-speech tag you have to supply.** Without the tag it defaults to noun and `better` stays `better`, which means **a lemmatiser used without tagging is a slower stemmer that happens to return real words.**

nodes.label: But the tag is an input

d.title: Format-specific cleaning is where the generic pipeline stops helping
d.caption: The eight generic stages do nothing about a `@mention`, a `#hashtag`, an `RT` prefix, a code block in a markdown document or a quoted reply chain in an email — **and each of those is a decision rather than a cleanup, because the thing you would strip is sometimes the signal.** A hashtag is the topic label on a tweet; a quoted reply is the context of the answer. **Which is why this stage cannot be a library default: it depends on the task, not the format.**

d.title: Six schemes, and only one of them can never say UNK
d.caption: Read the two ends against each other. **Word-level has a large vocabulary and handles an unseen word badly — it emits `[UNK]` and the information is gone. Byte-level BPE has the largest vocabulary of all and can never emit `[UNK]`**, because every input is a sequence of byte values and every byte value is in the table. Character-level gets the same guarantee with a ~256-symbol vocabulary, and pays for it in sequence length instead.

d.title: Three rounds, and the winner changes because the previous merge changed the counts
d.caption: The whole algorithm is in the third column. **Round 1 merges `u+g` at 20. That merge removes `(p,u)` from 17 down to 12, because five of those `pu` pairs were in `pug`, which is now `p·ug`** — so round 2's winner is `(u,n)` at 16 rather than the pair that was second a moment ago. **Each merge rewrites the frequency table it will be scored against next**, which is why BPE has to be run rather than predicted.

d.title: A word never seen, encoded from pieces that were
d.caption: **`bug` never appeared in training and still encodes cleanly as `b` + `ug`, because both pieces are in the vocabulary** — that is the property that makes subword tokenization work at all. And `mug` is the limit stated exactly: **`m` was never in the corpus, so there is no symbol for it**, which is what byte-level BPE fixes by making the base alphabet the 256 byte values instead of whatever characters happened to appear.

d.title: Make the alphabet the byte values and the problem stops existing
d.caption: A character-level base vocabulary **cannot represent text outside its training alphabet** — and `müller 😀` is exactly that text. As raw bytes it is `[109, 195, 188, 108, 108, 101, 114, 32, 240, 159, 152, 128]`, **and every one of those values is in 0..255**, so the base vocabulary covers all possible input by construction. **The cost is in the sequence: one character can take four bytes, so unusual text tokenises longer** — 10 tokens for 9 characters, measured below.

nodes.sub: so new characters have no symbol

nodes.label: So the base vocab covers everything
One character can be four bytes

d.title: The same table, two criteria, two different merges
d.caption: BPE takes the **count** and merges `(u,g)` at 20. WordPiece divides by how often the parts occur alone, **and `(g,s)` wins at 0.05 on a count of 5** — because `g` and `s` are rare on their own, so seeing them together is informative. **BPE asks “what is common”; WordPiece asks “what is surprisingly common”**, which is pointwise mutual information in all but name, and is why the two produce different vocabularies from identical text.

d.title: The same word through two real tokenizers, and one surprise
d.caption: BERT marks every continuation with `##`, so the pieces are visibly glued. GPT-2 marks the **space** instead, with `Ġ` — and that is the surprise worth keeping: **the real tokenizer produces `Ġtransformative` as one token, not ` transform` plus `ative`.** Which means a leading space is part of the token, so `'Hello world'` and `' Hello world'` tokenise differently: **in byte-level BPE, whitespace is data rather than a delimiter.**

d.title: Seven special tokens, and only one of them can break your model silently
d.caption: `[CLS]`, `[SEP]` and `[MASK]` are architectural — the pretraining objective is built around them, so using the wrong one fails loudly. **`[PAD]` is the dangerous one: it exists only to make a batch rectangular, and it must be masked out, or attention spends weight on positions that mean nothing** — which is a quiet accuracy loss rather than an error. And `[UNK]` is the row byte-level BPE deletes from the list entirely.

d.title: Three words, three vectors, and every pair is equally far apart
d.caption: The vectors are orthogonal, so **the dot product between any two distinct words is 0 and the cosine similarity is 0** — `cat` is exactly as unrelated to `kitten` as it is to `bulldozer`. That is the whole indictment: **one-hot encodes identity and nothing else, and the dimension is the vocabulary size**, so a 50,000-word vocabulary needs a 50,000-long vector to say *“this is word 3,112”*.

d.title: Sorted, de-duplicated, and order-free
d.caption: The feature list is **alphabetical and one entry per distinct word** — which is already the representation's two properties. Sorting means a column index has no relation to where the word appeared; de-duplication means a document is a point in a space with one axis per vocabulary word. **So “the dog chased the cat” and “the cat chased the dog” have identical vectors**, and no amount of counting recovers which one you had.

d.title: The word in every document gets an idf of exactly 1.0
d.caption: `the` has `df=3` in a three-document corpus, so `ln(3/3) + 1 = 1.0` — **the `+1` is the only reason it is not zero.** And then the arithmetic lands somewhere worth noticing: **`mat` at 0.3498 does beat `the` at 0.3333, but only just, because `the` appears twice and tf rewards that.** The raw formula divides by document length and does not renormalise, which is exactly where scikit-learn differs — and the difference matters.

d.title: The hand computation matches once you use the library's formula
d.caption: **`match: True`, and the row L2 norms are all exactly 1.0** — so two defaults are doing the work. `smooth_idf=True` computes `ln((1+N)/(1+df)) + 1`, as if one extra document contained every term, **which prevents a division by zero for a term seen at predict time but never in training.** And L2 normalisation scales every row to unit length, **so cosine similarity reduces to a dot product and document length stops mattering** — which is what fixed §03's near-tie.

d.title: Forty-one percent closer, which is less than the word “weighting” suggests
d.caption: This is the honest number: **the raw count ratio of `the` to `mat` is 2.0 and the tf-idf ratio is 1.181 — 41% closer, not eliminated.** `the` still outscores `mat` in doc 0. **idf compresses the gap between a common and a rare word; it does not invert it**, which is why `sublinear_tf` exists as the other half: it takes a hundredfold count difference down to 5.6-fold, because **the tenth occurrence of a word tells you far less than the first.**

d.title: Three representations, and the row that decides it
d.caption: **“Captures meaning” is the row that matters, and only the third column answers yes** — which is what the whole of 1.6 is about. The rest is a trade you can read off: the sparse representations are interpretable, cheap and exact, so a coefficient on `refund` is a number you can show someone; the dense one is none of those and knows that `refund` and `reimbursement` are related. **Neither of the first two columns can be fixed into the third by tuning.**
